solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Backed singular twit and deputy, as a concession to seniors?

indicators.note: something backed has been sent in the backward direction, so the whole string is read from its end

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
a sap is a fool
a sub, short for substitute, stands in for someone

explanation.surface: A dig at a foolish politician and his deputy, both apparently handed out like perks to pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' looks like 'supported', but it reverses everything that follows up to the definition. In Britain, pensioners get free local bus travel with such a pass.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain older people get free travel on local buses through a pass, a classic perk for pensioners.

clue.text: "Moreover, live with borders!"

blocks.note: to be is to exist, to live
the borders of something are its sides

explanation.surface: A rallying cry, perhaps for a nation learning to live with border controls again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' is the verb to exist, giving BE, not the adjective; 'with' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words introduce an additional point in an argument, functioning as sentence adverbs meaning 'in addition'.

clue.text: Lack drink? Drop dead!

blocks.note: a short is a small measure of spirits
to fall in battle is to drop dead

explanation.surface: Someone denied a drink snaps an insult back at the barman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop dead!' reads as a rude dismissal, but it is simply a verb meaning to fall and die. A short is British pub slang for a measure of spirits such as whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A deficit or deficiency, an amount by which supply falls below need, is the noun sense required.

clue.text: As jumpy as a TV presenter?

definitions.text: As jumpy as a TV presenter?

blocks.note: surface reading: restless and fidgety, the straight meaning of the word
setter's reading: like Ant, of the TV presenting duo Ant and Dec, with a -sy ending meaning 'like'

explanation.surface: A nervous broadcaster fidgeting in front of the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: Ant McPartlin is half of the British TV double act Ant and Dec, so being 'like Ant' reads as the informal word for restless.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal adjective means agitated, restless or nervous, the same as jumpy or fidgety.

clue.text: Smooth, failed presidential candidate's casual wear

blocks.note: to sand wood is to smooth it
Al Gore lost the 2000 US election, so 'his' is AL'S

explanation.surface: A slick losing politician dressed down in his off-duty clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' looks like an adjective for a slick candidate but is the verb to sand. The apostrophe-s is kept as an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Open summer footwear is informal clothing, so sandals are an example of relaxed attire.

clue.text: This is about restricting Rees-Mogg ultimately – which makes sense

definitions.note: the answer is one of the senses; the definition reads as a description

indicators.note: 'about' suggests turning things around and moving them, so these letters are rearranged
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is wanted
to restrict is to hem in, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: the four letters of the word rearranged
the final letter of the politician's surname

explanation.surface: A sardonic remark that limiting Jacob Rees-Mogg is the only sensible policy.
explanation.walkthrough: THIS is jumbled to SIHT and the G from Rees-Mogg goes inside it. 'This' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision is one of the five human senses, so it is a thing that 'makes sense' in the most literal way.

clue.text: Butt removed from Ozzie bloke – tough

indicators.note: a butt is the end of something, so with it taken away the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: Strine is Australian English, minus its last letter
a gent is a man

explanation.surface: An Australian man has had his backside chopped off and is coping manfully.
explanation.walkthrough: Strine is a jokey name for the Australian accent and dialect, from 'Australian' said quickly; 'Ozzie' looks like a man's nickname but stands for that dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: Strict, demanding or severe rules are stringent, matching tough in the sense of hard to satisfy.

clue.text: Pulverize Labour!

blocks.note: first meaning: crush into powder
second meaning: hard monotonous work

explanation.walkthrough: The capital L makes 'Labour' look like the political party being crushed; it is just hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to crush to powder, and the noun means tedious, exhausting toil, as in the daily routine.

clue.text: (& 21dn.) Fasten Hoey to ground, as a sample of how better life could be!

definitions.text: a sample of how better life could be

indicators.note: ground means milled to bits, so the letters are broken up and reformed

blocks.note: the three words supply all twelve letters

explanation.surface: A call to pin down Kate Hoey, the Labour Brexiteer MP, as a foretaste of the good life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fasten' and 'ground' look like instructions for tethering someone, but 'ground' is the anagram signal. Kate Hoey was a Labour MP.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief experience of sweetness hints at greater pleasures to come; it is also the title of a famous play.

clue.text: Bill, the controversial presenter is over

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
Jonathan Ross, a broadcaster often in trouble

explanation.surface: A TV host's career, or a bill, is declared finished.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Ross is a British TV and radio presenter whose prank-call scandal caused outrage. 'Bill' looks like a name but is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: Both prepositions mean on the far side of, as in going over or across a road.

clue.text: Devious USSR chlorinated Bush?

indicators.note: devious means winding and crooked, so the letters take a twisted route

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Cold War paranoia: the Soviets secretly poisoned President Bush with chlorine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' looks like the American president but is slang for pubic hair. The short and curlies are pubic hairs, as in 'got by the short and curlies'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pubic hair is called a bush in slang, and this British phrase names the same body hair humorously.

clue.text: Pointed nuts

blocks.note: first meaning: marked with dots or points
second meaning: crazy, eccentric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointed nuts' suggests sharp-tipped kernels; instead each word separately defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spotted with dots is literally covered in points, while the informal sense means slightly mad or eccentric.

clue.text: That's owing to Auden, um, being drunk

definitions.note: 'that which is owing', a noun phrase

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: nine letters from the three words

explanation.surface: An excuse that a hesitant speaker's debt is down to the poet W. H. Auden's boozing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Owing to' looks like the phrase meaning 'because of', but 'to' belongs to the fodder and 'That's owing' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The sum someone still has to pay on a bill is the money outstanding, i.e. what is still owed.

clue.text: Briny members found by experienced sailors

definitions.note: a description of the answer rather than a synonym

blocks.note: the briny is a nickname for the sea
limbs are members of the body

explanation.surface: Salty limbs discovered among seasoned mariners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' looks like members of a crew, but here it means limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Seasoned mariners develop the balance to walk steadily on a rolling ship, which is what this phrase describes.

clue.text: Male line buggered when one enters battle location

indicators.note: buggered is slang for broken or ruined, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: the eight letters as printed
A means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: A family's line of male heirs ruined when one goes off to war.
explanation.walkthrough: The A joins the fodder before shuffling; reading 'one' as I does not work, since the answer needs a second A.
explanation.definitionFit: El Alamein in Egypt was the site of a decisive 1942 Allied victory over Rommel in the desert war.

clue.text: Repulsed, National Front takes sod all in back payments

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside another
placed in means put inside, so this combination goes within the next piece
going back means travelling in the reverse direction, so the word is read from the end

blocks.note: the far-right British party's initials
sod all is British slang for nothing, i.e. zero
fees are charges paid

explanation.surface: The National Front gets nothing in back pay and is sent packing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back payments' looks like arrears but splits into a reversal signal and its fodder. Two containers nest: the O goes into the party's initials first, then that goes into the reversed fees.
explanation.definitionFit: To see off an attacker or rival is to drive them away successfully, so repulsed fits as a past participle.

clue.text: Preoccupation of conference of former Etonians, say, in short

blocks.note: Old Boys abbreviated; Old Etonians are one example
a session is a sitting or meeting

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Tory conference is fixated on its Old Etonian members.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Etonians are former pupils of Eton, the elite English school; old boys of any school are OBs, with 'say' marking Etonians as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixation or compulsive interest that fills the mind, as a preoccupation does, is the synonym needed.

clue.text: Ruler's mate ballsed up tuna salad – plug pulled

indicators.note: something pulled has been withdrawn, so those letters are taken out
ballsed up is slang for messed up, so the remaining letters are put in disorder

blocks.note: the nine letters as printed
a plug is a promotional advert, an AD

explanation.surface: A king's consort botches a tuna salad and the blender's plug gets yanked.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove AD from TUNA SALAD and rearrange the seven letters left. 'Plug pulled' sounds like cutting the power, but plug means an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: A sultan's wife is a sultana, so she is the consort, the partner, of that Muslim monarch.

clue.text: Stuff Labour leaders, Brown and rest

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words
umber is a brown earth pigment

explanation.surface: A curse on the Labour leadership, Gordon Brown included, and everyone else besides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown, but it is the colour; 'Labour leaders' wants to be Starmer or Brown, yet it takes initials from 'Stuff Labour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep is a form of repose, and the noun names a peaceful sleep, the same as rest.

clue.text: 'Nassau tum' naturally partly responsible for fall

indicators.note: partly means only in part, so the answer is a run of letters inside the words

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: A paunch acquired in the Bahamas sunshine is half to blame for someone's tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: Fall is the American word for the season, so the definition is a noun, not the verb the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Fall is the North American name for the season between summer and winter.

clue.text: Ousted leader makes meek sound, squeezing false tits

indicators.note: false means fake or not genuine, so the letters are not in their true order
to squeeze something is to press it inside a grip, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: the bleat of a sheep, the meekest of animals
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A deposed dictator gives a timid bleat while clutching a pair of fake breasts.
explanation.walkthrough: Fulgencio Batista was the Cuban dictator overthrown by Castro in 1959. A sheep's bleat stands for meekness, as in 'meek as a lamb'.
explanation.definitionFit: Batista was the Cuban head of state removed from power by revolution, so he is a deposed ruler.

clue.text: eBay not working? Stick it!

definitions.note: the verb: stab with a blade

indicators.note: something working is in motion and being processed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the seven letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A frustrated user tells the auction website where to put it when it crashes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not working' reads as one phrase meaning broken, but 'not' is fodder and 'working' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To bayonet someone is to stab them with the blade fixed to a rifle, so it means to stick it into them.

clue.text: Andy, one to go mad, gets pissed

definitions.note: US slang, short for pissed off

indicators.note: going mad means losing order and sense, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: as printed
as printed

explanation.surface: Andy, about to lose it, gets drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English 'pissed' usually means drunk, the surface sense; here it is the American sense of angry.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang pissed means angry or irritated, which is a close synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Invalid male interrupting Hunt? Lay off!

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of place, so the letters are reordered
to interrupt is to break into something, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: he is the male pronoun
the seven letters of the two words rearranged

explanation.surface: A plea to leave health secretary Jeremy Hunt alone when a sick man barges in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' looks like the noun for a sick person but works as the adjective. Jeremy Hunt was the British health secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as an adjective, invalid (stress on the first syllable) means sickly or in poor health.

clue.text: see 7dn.
Boris's dodgy name for Queen – "shaggy thing"

indicators.note: 'X for Y' means X stands in the place of Y, so one letter swaps for another
dodgy means unreliable or shifty, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: as printed
N is the abbreviation for name
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson's disrespectful nickname for the monarch, with a nod to his own messy hair.
explanation.walkthrough: N replaces the R in BORIS, giving BONIS, which is then rearranged. The 's reads as 'is', a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: The American buffalo is covered in a thick coat of long, matted hair, making it a famously shaggy animal.

clue.text: Very good support for a bust ball pinching vein opening

indicators.note: an opening is the very start, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: a bra supports the bust
the first letter of the word
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Applause for a sturdy bra on a busted ball gown, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' here means grabbing, so the ball picks up V in front of it rather than wrapping round it. 'Bust' wants to be broken, but it is the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian exclamation is shouted as praise, much as one says 'well done' or 'very good'.

clue.text: Defensive attitude: Hitler's ultimate mindset?

blocks.note: first meaning: a siege mindset of feeling under attack
second meaning: literally the frame of mind of a man holed up in his Berlin shelter at the end

explanation.walkthrough: Hitler spent his final days in the Führerbunker, so his last state of mind was literally that of someone in a bunker.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a group that sees itself besieged by enemies and refuses outside criticism.

clue.text: Flash: our national leaders' fake material

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: a ray is a beam or flash of light
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A complaint that the country's top politicians are a flashy, synthetic sham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like an adjective meaning showy, but it is a noun for a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is a man-made fibre made from cellulose, once marketed as artificial silk.

clue.text: Prickly Edward nursing erection

indicators.note: to nurse is to cradle something in the arms, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: Ted is a short form of Edward
horn is slang for an erection

explanation.surface: An irritable Edward with an embarrassing condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prickly' looks like a description of Edward's mood but is the definition; Edward must be shortened to its familiar form before anything goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Covered with sharp spines like a rose stem, which is the literal sense of prickly.
